title: Factores que influyen en compartir noticias falsas de salud online / Factors that influence sharing online fake news on health
screen_reason: Two-wave national panel survey of Chilean internet users. The descriptive section (Table 1, wave 2, 2018) reports, for each of four specific false health news stories that had circulated in Chile, the share of respondents who said they had been exposed to it (65.2%-75.4%) and the share who said they had shared it on their social networks (5.0%-18.2%). Both are shares of survey respondents reporting encounter and self-reported actual (not hypothetical) sharing, i.e. RECALL under §1. The regression models are the paper's aim but the descriptive table is what makes it eligible.

estimates.platform: online survey panel; exposure not tied to a named platform (Facebook used by 90% of participants)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who said they had been exposed to each of four specific false health news stories circulating in Chile
estimates.value_raw: 65,2% (milk is not nourishing and can be harmful), 69,7% (genetically modified food is harmful), 72,3% (vaccines cause autism), 75,4% (vaccines can be more harmful than the disease) — Tabla 1, column 'Exposición'
estimates.denominator: 451 Chilean internet users who completed wave 2 (June 2018) of a panel stratified on the national CASEN survey by sex, age and geography; wave 1 (April 2017) invited 8,840 and obtained 1,007 responses
estimates.definition: respondent said they had been exposed to (had seen) the specific false health news story, which the researchers had pre-selected as false and as having circulated in Chile in the preceding 15 months
estimates.misinfo_def: "noticias que no tienen una base objetiva, pero que se presentan como noticias" [news that has no objective basis but is presented as news] (Allcott & Gentzkow, 2017, p. 5)
estimates.source_quote: personas mostraron un porcentaje alto de conocimiento de estas noticias, ya que dijeron haber sido expuestas entre un 65,2% y un 75,4% de las veces.
estimates.page_loc: Sect. 4.1 Análisis descriptivo and Tabla 1, p. 6
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-report: exposure and sharing are both reported by the respondent. IMPORTANT NUANCE - the VERACITY of the stimulus is not left to the respondent: the researchers pre-selected four named health stories known to be false and known to have circulated in Chile in the previous 15 months, and asked whether the respondent had seen and had shared each one. So this is item-level recall of pre-designated false claims, a stronger design than a generic 'have you seen misinformation' item; ground_truth is coded self_report per the schema rule for RECALL, but an adjudicator should read it as researcher-fixed veracity plus self-reported encounter. No fact-checker is named as the source of the falsity determination, and no coder count or reliability statistic is given. Self-reported exposure is subject to recall error and to false recognition.
estimates.moderator_quote: Los participantes fueron expuestos a 4 noticias falsas en el área de la salud, que habían circulado en Chile los 15 meses anteriores, para luego ser consultados si las habían compartido en sus redes sociales. [Participants were shown 4 false news stories in the health area that had circulated in Chile in the previous 15 months, and were then asked whether they had shared them on their social networks.]
estimates.notes: value_kind = range_not_point because the paper reports FOUR item-level percentages and NO pooled figure; averaging them would be a forbidden cross-category computation under R8, and the authors' own headline sentence states the result as a range. All four point values are preserved verbatim in value_raw so an adjudicator can pool them if the review's convention allows item-level rows: 65.2 / 69.7 / 72.3 / 75.4. Note the two vaccine items (72.3%, 75.4%) are the two highest; topic is coded health_other because the four-item set mixes vaccines (2 items) with nutrition/GMO (2 items). English translation of source_quote: 'Table 1 shows that people displayed a high percentage of familiarity with this news, since they said they had been exposed to it between 65.2% and 75.4% of the time.' Confidence medium: the wording of the exposure item is never given, and the table's percentages are stated without counts, so they cannot be checked against 451. On the source_quote: truncated at the start because a pull-quote box ('Las noticias falsas en salud fueron altamente conocidas por las personas, quienes estuvieron expuestas entre un 65,2% y un 75,4% de las veces') is interleaved into the sentence in the extracted text; the sentence begins 'En tabla 1 se observa que las'.

estimates.platform: respondents' own social networks (redes sociales; Facebook used by 90% of participants), measured by survey self-report
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who said they had shared each of four specific false health news stories on their social networks
estimates.value_raw: 10,6% (milk is not nourishing and can be harmful), 18,2% (genetically modified food is harmful), 5,0% (vaccines cause autism), 8,7% (vaccines can be more harmful than the disease) — Tabla 1, column 'La compartí'
estimates.denominator: 451 Chilean internet users who completed wave 2 (June 2018) of a CASEN-stratified national panel; the table gives no counts, and the paper does not state explicitly whether the sharing percentage is of ALL respondents or only of those exposed
estimates.definition: respondent said they had shared the specific false health news story on their social networks (self-reported past behaviour, not intention)
estimates.misinfo_def: "noticias que no tienen una base objetiva, pero que se presentan como noticias" [news that has no objective basis but is presented as news] (Allcott & Gentzkow, 2017, p. 5)
estimates.source_quote: Es interesante resaltar que los porcentajes de aquellos que, finalmente, compartieron estas noticias son aún más bajos, alcanzando la noticia que más se compartió sólo el 18,2%.
estimates.page_loc: Sect. 4.1 Análisis descriptivo and Tabla 1, p. 6
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-report: exposure and sharing are both reported by the respondent. IMPORTANT NUANCE - the VERACITY of the stimulus is not left to the respondent: the researchers pre-selected four named health stories known to be false and known to have circulated in Chile in the previous 15 months, and asked whether the respondent had seen and had shared each one. So this is item-level recall of pre-designated false claims, a stronger design than a generic 'have you seen misinformation' item; ground_truth is coded self_report per the schema rule for RECALL, but an adjudicator should read it as researcher-fixed veracity plus self-reported encounter. No fact-checker is named as the source of the falsity determination, and no coder count or reliability statistic is given. Self-reported sharing is likely under-reported (social desirability) and is not validated against any platform trace.
estimates.moderator_quote: De estas respuestas creamos una sola variable, que fue compartir noticias falsas de salud (rango = 0 [ninguna noticia fue compartida] a 4 [compartió todas las noticias]. [From these answers we created a single variable, sharing false health news (range = 0 [no story shared] to 4 [shared all the stories]).]
estimates.notes: This is SELF-REPORTED sharing, so it is RECALL with recall_subtype = sharing, NOT the SHARING construct (which §3 reserves for observed platform data). value_kind = range_not_point for the same reason as the exposure row: four item-level values, no pooled figure, and averaging is barred. Point values preserved: 10.6 / 18.2 / 5.0 / 8.7. English translation of source_quote: 'It is interesting to note that the percentages of those who finally shared this news are even lower, with the most-shared story reaching only 18.2%.' AMBIGUITY FOR THE ADJUDICATOR: whether the sharing percentage is a share of all 451 respondents or a share of those who reported exposure. The measurement section ('Los participantes fueron expuestos a 4 noticias falsas ... para luego ser consultados si las habían compartido') and the ordering exposure > credibility > shared both point to all respondents, and I have coded it that way; if it were conditional on exposure the values would be roughly 7-26% instead. Related but separate: the composite sharing scale has M = 0.60 (wave 1) and M = 0.43 (wave 2) on a 0-4 count of stories shared, which is a per-capita intensity, not a share.

missed_or_uncertain: Seen and deliberately NOT extracted: (1) The credibility column of Tabla 1 — 29.6%, 46.8%, 17.5%, 26.7% of respondents rated each false story 'quite credible' or 'very credible'. This is BELIEF in false claims, which §1 excludes explicitly. It is the paper's best-predicting variable but it is not exposure. (2) The composite dependent variable 'compartir noticias falsas de salud', a 0-4 count of how many of the four stories the respondent shared, M = 0.60 (wave 1, alpha .68) and M = 0.43 (wave 2, alpha .59) — a mean count, not a share; it could in principle be a per_capita_intensity row but its unit (stories out of a fixed set of four) is not comparable to a diet or exposure count, so I left it out and record it here instead. (3) All regression coefficients in Tabla 2 (attention to health news beta = .101; trust in contacts .099; trust in media -.101; credibility in fake news .170) — predictors of sharing, not prevalence. (4) Scale means for attention (M = 3.51), trust in contacts (M = 2.33), trust in media (M = 2.99), credibility (M = 2.7) — scale means with no threshold share. (5) Figures cited from elsewhere, barred by R8: 'las noticias falsas tienen un 70% más de probabilidades de ser re-tweeteadas que aquellas que son verdaderas' [false news is 70% more likely to be retweeted than true news] (MIT, via Kari 2018) and the speculation that 'para el año 2022, la mitad de las noticias online serán falsas' [by 2022 half of online news will be false] (Ponce 2018). (6) Sample composition (56.8% women, 90% Facebook use) — not misinformation.

rob.design: Two-wave online panel survey of Chilean internet users, wave 1 April 2017 and wave 2 June 2018. Panel built using the stratification of Chile's national CASEN socio-economic survey on sex, age and geography, described by the authors as nationally representative. Wave 1: 8,840 invited, 1,007 responded (11.4% response). Wave 2: 451 responded (45% of wave-1 respondents; roughly 5% of those originally invited) — attrition is severe and no attrition analysis is reported. Predictors taken from wave 1 and the dependent variable from wave 2, analysed with lagged-dependent-variable OLS (4 hierarchical models, adjusted R2 25.3%-28.9%). Everything is self-report; sharing is not validated against platform data. Composite sharing scale alpha = .68 (wave 1) and .59 (wave 2) — the wave-2 alpha is below conventional thresholds. Table 1 reports percentages without counts, so the descriptive figures cannot be reconstructed from n = 451. Stimulus falsity rests on the authors' selection with no stated fact-check source.
